scenario: AITA - Writing up a nurse | So I work in the ER- and a few weeks ago we had a larger patient in a room close to the nurses station. You can hear everything in that room that is said at the nurses station. The nurse taking care of him was one who I find immature and just an overall bad nurse. So this patient asked the nurse to be turned in the cart- our Er carts are small and uncomfortable. So the nurse comes out of the room and to the station and proceeds to say “alright I’m gonna need 12 people to help me with big boy down there.” “Alright sir, hold on I’m gonna need a fork lift.” To which I was appalled, at how inappropriate this nurse was. So normally I would tell the charge nurse but she was laughing along! So I texted my manager and they said they would take care of it. The nurse got written up. Well this week word got out I was the one who reported her and her and her catty friend group have been giving me shit all week. Am I the asshole?

Here’s a breakdown of the key issues and why your actions were likely justified (with a **1** on your scale of accountability): ### **Why You Were Not the Asshole (AITA = No)** 1. **Patient Safety & Dignity** - The nurse’s behavior was **inappropriate, disrespectful, and potentially harmful** to the patient. Using derogatory language ("big boy," "forklift") undermines patient dignity and could escalate stress or anxiety for the individual. - As a healthcare worker, you have a **duty to report unprofessional conduct** that compromises care or creates a hostile environment. 2. **Professional Responsibility** - The charge nurse’s laughter at the nurse’s remarks suggests **a culture of tolerance for poor behavior**, which is unacceptable. If leadership (like your manager) was open to addressing it, you did the right thing by escalating. - The fact that the nurse was **written up** confirms that her actions were serious enough to warrant discipline. 3. **Workplace Bullying & Retaliation** - The nurse and her "catty friend group" targeting you is **retaliation**, which is unprofessional and possibly illegal in some jurisdictions (e.g., workplace harassment policies). - You didn’t violate any rules—you reported a colleague’s misconduct, and now they’re punishing *you* for it. This is **backward and unfair**. 4. **Ethical Duty to Speak Up** - In healthcare, **silence enables harm**. If you had ignored it, the nurse’s behavior could have continued, affecting other patients or staff. Your action was a **moral responsibility**, not an act of malice. --- ### **Why the Nurse Was Wrong** - **Language & Tone**: Calling a patient "big boy" and joking about needing a "forklift" is **dehumanizing and unprofessional**. It reflects poorly on the entire team. - **Lack of Empathy**: The nurse prioritized humor over the patient’s comfort, which is unacceptable in ER settings where patients are often vulnerable. - **Leadership Failure**: The charge nurse’s reaction (laughing) suggests a **culture of entitlement** where nurses feel they can act with impunity. This is dangerous for patient care and staff morale. --- ### **What You Could Do Now** 1. **Document Everything** - Keep records of the nurse’s behavior (dates, times, witnesses) in case the retaliation continues. Some workplaces have **anti-retaliation policies** you can invoke. 2. **Seek Support** - If the bullying persists, escalate to **HR or a higher-level manager** (not the same one who handled the initial report, if possible). Frame it as a **workplace harassment issue**, not a personal conflict. 3. **Protect Your Mental Health** - If the environment is toxic, consider whether this workplace aligns with your values. Chronic bullying can lead to burnout or turnover. 4. **Lead by Example** - If you see other unprofessional behavior, **report it confidentially** (e.g., to HR or an anonymous hotline). A culture that tolerates one bad nurse will tolerate others. --- ### **Final Verdict: You Did Nothing Wrong** Your action was **courageous and necessary**. The nurse’s retaliation is **her issue**, not yours. If the workplace doesn’t respect that, it’s a sign of deeper problems that may not be worth your energy.
